L0@P0: TIRE BUYERS’ FAQ—
L1@P0: WHAT YOU SHOULD KNOW AND ASK
L2@P0: The next time you’re in the market to buy tires, be sure to print out these Tire Buyer FAQs to equip
L3@P0: yourself with key purchasing information about tires.
L4@P0: What type of tire should I buy?
L5@P0: This will vary by where you live and the typical weather you drive in.
L6@P0:  All-season tires can handle a variety of road conditions. They have some mud and snow
L7@P0: capabilities.
L8@P0:  Winter tires are more effective than all-season tires in deep snow.
L9@P0:  Summer tires are warm-weather tires that are not designed to operate in temperatures below
L10@P0: freezing, or on snow and ice.
L11@P0:  All-terrain tires are mainly used on four-wheel drive vehicles. They provide a good compromise
L12@P0: between on-road driving and off-road capability.
L13@P0: What size tires should I buy?
L14@P0: Check your owner’s manual or the Tire and Loading Information Label located on the
L15@P0: driver’s side door edge or post to find the correct size for your car or truck.
L16@P0: How are tires rated? What does the tire rating mean?
L17@P0: Many tires are rated by the U.S. Government on treadwear, traction performance and temperature resistance. It’s called the
L18@P0: Uniform Tire Quality Grading Standards (UTQGS) (PDF 5 MB), and the tire ratings are on the sidewall of every passenger vehicle tire
L19@P0: sold in the United States.
L20@P0:  Treadwear grades tell you how long the tread should last. For example, tires with a grade of 200 should wear twice as a long
L21@P0: as a tire with a grade of 100. The tread on tires with highest numeric ratings, 600 or more, should take longer to wear down.
L22@P0:  Traction grades tell you the tire’s ability to allow a car to stop on wet pavement in a shorter distance. It’s graded AA, A, B or
L23@P0: C, with AA being the highest rating.
L24@P0:  Temperature grades tell you how well the tire resists heat. It’s graded A, B or C, with A being the highest rating.
L25@P0: How old is the tire I’m buying?
L26@P0: All tires have a DOT Tire Identification Number
L27@P0: (TIN) on the sidewall. The last four digits
L28@P0: represent the week and year the tire was made.
L29@P0: NHTSA recommends checking this date when
L30@P0: purchasing tires, along with knowing the vehicle
L31@P0: manufacturer’s recommended tire replacement
L32@P0: timeframe. Look on both sides of the tire. The TIN
L33@P0: may not be on both sides.
